subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deem it
my duty t-o take part in such an important debate as the one now engrossing the attention of the House, especially when I note the enthusiasm with which the budget has been received. There is no doubt that this budget
has brought relief to all the homes; however, on the other hand, it has spread confusion in the ranks of our opponents. The best evidence of this can be found in the speeches of the hon. members for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who, forced to admit the prosperity of our country, find no other justification than to ascribe this prosperity to Providence. It is a fact, Sir, that Providence has been especially kind to us, but our hon. friends forget the old proverb, which is always true:	Help yourself
and God will help you. Ever since the present government have assumed power, they have given proof of moderation and especially of economy in the administration of public affairs. They succeeded in wiping out the endless deficits which took place under the Conservative regime-in this instance Providence came to our rescue-while under the Conservative rule we have never known anything else but bad administration, wild and foolish expenditure. There is, therefore, nothing astonishing that Providence did not lavish its favours on such a government.
I am overjoyed with the budget. I spoke, a moment ago, of the relief which it has brought in the homes. I wish now to say a few words about the cutting down of the income tax. To-day, owing to this reduction, every home and in particular every individual will be able to set aside a good deal of savings. Indeed, not only do we reduce, but a remedy is applied to a state of things which was in the past entirely unjust; we discriminate as between the earned and the unearned income. It was unfair that a man who had but his salary to live on or to provide for the needs of his family, should be placed on the same footing as the one who drew the same income, but derived it from dividends or inheritance. To-day, we assess the income with more fairness. The doing away with the stamp duty on receipts is also an excellent measure.
Another very popular measure throughout the country is the return to the penny postage rate. On and after July 1, 1926, instead of 3 cents the postage fees on letters in Canada and to the United States will be but 2 cents, that is a saving of 33 per cent, Everybody will admit that it is quite an appreciable reduction.
Another item in the budget which meets with my entire approval, is the tariff reduction on automobiles. I live in a district where this means of travelling is at present, spreading more and more. The automobile is no more considered an object of luxury, but is in daily use, owing to the precious saving of time which we realize. As this reduction

The Budget-Mr. Sylvestre
applies to low price cars, it is again a popular measure, because it especially affects the mass. When I see manufacturers organize delegations, regardless of expense, in order to come and tell us that on account of such reduction -of so little moment-they will be forced to close their factories, I cannot, Sir, believe in the sincerity of these people, for I am not aware that the profits which the manufacturers make go to the people; they rather go to a priviledged class of society. No, this reduction will not be the cause of the closing of these factories. On the contrary, there will be a compensation owing to the increased number of sales.
It also affords me pleasure to discuss the important question of our railways. By a subtle intellectual effort, the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) tried to ascribe to his leader, the one who, at present, guides the policy of the opposition, all the merit of the good management of the state railways. It is quite true, that it was under the rule of the leader of the opposition that the National railways were purchased, however, the hon. member forgot to mention the fabulous and fantastic price paid for a heap of old scrap iron and an entirely depreciated stock. We should rather congratulate the government on its judicious choice in selecting Sir Henry Thornton for the management of our railways, who, thanks to his able management, obtains magnificent results, to such an extent that these railways instead of being a burden to the state will before long be a source of revenue. And while on the subject, allow me to refer to something which especially interests the portion of the population which I represent in this House.
The county of Lake St. John located beyond this granite wall which is called the Laurentides, is reached only by the National railways. Half, at least, of the population of my county is at a distance of ten, fifteen, forty and even fifty miles from the railway. There is no need of further emphasizing this fact-since I represent an entirely farming community-in order to point out not only all the disadvantages and inconveniences which result, but also the necessity incumbent on the government railway to encircle with rails the county I represent. And that is what I beg the government to do. The time of evading the issue has passed 1 Too long have the farmers and settlers waited! Too long have the farmers and settlers of my county borne the burden! The time has come to grant them what they ask and I shall only cease insisting on my claim when this object has been attained.

Last night I listened attentively to the speech of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Smoke). I must acknowledge that he had at least the frankness of expressing his views when so many of his freinds, in the opposition, share these views but dare not express them. He stated that he had noticed that there existed in the province of Quebec a certain antagonism against the province of Ontario. My good friend is very much ill informed. It is evident that he has never visited our province or he would express himself otherwise. I especially extend an invitation to him to visit us and if he accepts, he will meet a busy, hard-working and sympathetic people; he will meet a law-abiding people; finally, he will meet this good old French cheerfulness, as well as the smile which is seen only among our own people and impossible, Sir, to find on the faces of those who sit in the opposition.

hear!

speechtext:
At the
outset of this session, the sympathetic and distinguished member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard), in a brief speech, paid a very high compliment to the French Canadians. It is always delightful to hear people sharing neither our faith nor our language, speaking about us in praiseworthy terms. The hon. member for Sherbrooke lives among us and he has learned to respect us instead of despising us. Is this not the best example of tolerance which can be found? I do not think that it is an easy task to find many such cases in the other provinces. Although not belonging to the same faith or race as ours, the hon. member for Sherbrooke, nevertheless, represents a county of which three-fourths are French Canadian, and I admit that never has this county been better advised than in choosing the member who, at present, so worthily represents it. That is why I state:	No antagonism whatsoever exists in
our province against the province of Ontario. We are proud of our province, we are proud of our country. When I listen, for instance, to certain patriotic statements of my friends in the opposition, I would be inclined to believe that they alone love their country. I am not aware, however, that the opposition have a monopoly of all virtues and learning. I might retort: We also love our country but not in the same way. With your exaggerated high protective policy, you only think of the large interests, while we-I am not a freetrader, I rather place my trust in a moderate protective policy-love our country in a

The Budget-Mr. Stinson
different manner because we concern ourselves with every class of society. We do want our industries to prosper. They prospered under our rule and they will still prosper; however, we want the small wage earner to also have his share of happiness in this country; we wish to protect him and we come to his relief by reducing the tariff and helping him in every possible way. And I am convinced, Sir, that our love, if it is less demonstrative than that of the opposition, is certainly more to the point, for instead of contenting ourselves with uttering high-sounding statements, we use means which bring results. That is why I am convinced that, under the present rule, we are but at the dawn of our expansion, we are but at the beginning of an era of prosperity which will ever increase. For, it cannot be denied, it is self-evident, from one end of the country to the other, from ocean to ocean, there reigns an epoch of prosperity unknown for a long time past. It is not by appealing to race prejudices; it is not by attempting to set up classes, one against the other, that we will accomplish the most useful work; but it is simply by advocating closer ties, by asking that, throughout Canada, people perform the same good work as practised in our province, for in Quebec all races come into contact daily without any friction whatsoever, in Quebec all religious denominations carry on without people insulting one another. That is why, the day-to which we all aspire-when conditions which prevail in our province will have become general throughout, Canada, we shall become a united nation, we shall form a whole, concentrating all our efforts-the common daily effort-towards the same goal, the same ideal, which consists in the development and expansion of our country, thus shall we succeed in making it greater, more beautiful, more united and more prosperous.
Mr. T. H. STINSON (Victoria, Ont.); Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to congratulate the Finance minister (Mr. Robb) for the comprehensive way in which he has presented the budget. It is clear in most parts, contains some jokers in others, but on the whole it does not offer to the country the Christmas tree that the Speech from the Throne contained for our Progressive friends.
I believe in giving credit where credit is due. We thank the minister for some reduction in taxes. The receipt tax is gone, for which we are truly grateful. That tax was always a tax in the line of a nuisance. I think that he would have been well advised if he had abolished the cheque tax also, and left the postage rate as it is. The cheque
tax retards business, and everything that stands in the way of holding back business should be removed as far as possible, with the hope of developing business and creating employment for our people. The postage reduction we appreciate, but the saving will not fill the dinner pails of many people in Canada, and I trust that the minister will not take part of those savings out of the pockets of the poorly paid postmasters. I want to read an extract from the letter of a country postmaster in my riding touching on this question. He says:
I would like to draw your attention to the statement in the paper re two-cent postage. It is coming to the people all right, but there is no statement as to how they are going to treat your postmasters. As you know, all post-masters are paid on commission. If Mr. Robb takes one-third of their salary away, how does he expect them to carry on?
I would be glad if the Minister of Finance would keep them in mind, and do something for these poorly paid postmasters throughout the country districts.
The income tax reductions will not afford relief to very many actually requiring relief at the present time. The ordinary workman is not now paying income tax. We appreciate the reductions, but I am afraid that the changes are going to do more harm than good; certainly they will seriously operate against Canadian industry. The fundamental principle that money should only be taxed once by the same government is taken away by this amendment. When invested in Canadian corporations the income of the company is taxed nine per cent. When passed on in dividends, it is again taxed in the hands of the shareholders. This is going to make it difficult to get money to finance new enterprises in Canada. It will have the effect of forcing capital into foreign investments, capital that is badly needed for development purposes in Canada. The proposed amendment will be particularly hard on a certain class of well-to-do farmers who have put their money into co-operative enterprises, such as elevators, flour mills, seed and grain businesses. The company will pay to the government nine per cent on its income, and the dividends when distributed are taxed again in the hands of the shareholders, while the non-incorporated company or man, in opposition to the farmers' company, only pays the one tax.
Clause 11 provides that where a corporation having undistributed income redeems its shares at a premium, the premium shall be taxed as a dividend against the shareholders. Such a regulation would seemingly disrupt the entire stock market, on shares listed at over par and which are subject to call at a price
The Budget-Mr. Stinson

over par. These shares may be sold four or five times on the market during the year, and to determine who is to pay that tax is going to be a difficult question. Let me read an extract from the Financial Post in its issue of April 23:
"It's a fine day; let's go out and kill something," is the reputed watchword cxf the sporting Britisher. "It's a prosperous period; let's go out and stop some of the prosperity," is the condensed substance of the Hon. Mr. Robb's budget, delivered just after we went to press last week. Most Canadians had not realized how prosperous the country was, until Mr. Robb had, so to speak, "drawn a bead" on that prosperity.
The reductions in the income tax are admirable. That is, they would be if the revenue thus lost to the Exchequer were being made up from any proper source. But the proposal to impose a special tax on corporate profits, over and above all ordinary taxation of the company's business and of the incomes of its proprietors-a tax on the company for being a Canadian company and nothing else-is so astounding that for a long time we were unable to believe that this was what the government intended to enact.
Next we come to the question of reduction in the motor duties, which brings up the whole question of the tariff and what our policy should be as it vitally affects the whole Dominion of Canada. The problem of the tariff has been one of the most persistent and controversial in Canadian history, affecting as is does the well-being and prosperity, directly or indirectly, of every citizen. When Canada was New France the control of trade and commerce was vested in the king alone. It led to excessive favouritism and caused a tremendous amount of smuggling, while trade itself was almost at a standstill-and apparently history is repeating itself, according to the evidence that is coming out at the customs probe these days. In the early days of British rule the regulation and division of customs duties was the source of bitter quarrels between Ontario and Quebec. In 1869 Canada asserted definite control of her tariff _ problems when Sir Alexander J. Galt made a firm declaration of Canada's right to regulate her own tariff, and Great Britain at once acquiesced. Since confederation the tariff has been a leading political issue, with the announcement in 1878 by Sir John A. Macdonald of a National Policy " to benefit and foster agriculture, mining, manufacturing, labour and other interests of the Dominion."
With Sir John A. Macdonald's success in the elections of 1878 Canada became a protectionist country. It is significant testimony to his vision and foresight that since then no political party, until recently, has ever advocated complete free trade as the proper course of action for Canada. We have had cries of " low tariff ", " commercial union " with the United States, or " reciprocity," but never " free trade " as a party slogan, but

the present Progressive group from the west have in the back of their minds free trade, as expressed by some of them. As early as 1876 Sir Wilfrid Laurier declared himself a moderate protectionist, admitting that protection was a matter of necessity for a young nation in order that it might obtain the full development of its own resources. When the Liberals came to power in 1896, after eighteen weary years in the wilderness, there was no real change in the tariff except for the preference extended to Great Britain. The lapse from orthodoxy in the ill-timed reciprocity plan of 1911 was decisively rejected by the country. During the war period the only alteration in the tariff was a sur-tax imposed for special war revenue. Thus from 1878 to 1921 Canada, with the general approval of her people, was a moderately protectionist countiy. Since that time the altered aspect of the political scene has made the tariff problem a serious and disturbing one.
WTith the formation of the farmers' or Progressive party a strong group appeared in 1921-since materially diminished-advocating a new national policy which included, (1) a wide extension of the free list; (2) free trade with Great Britain within five years, and (3) a general all-round reduction of duties. That party had gathered around it the doctrinaire free traders, some labour groups which the general post-war depression had hit hard, and some farm groups. The Liberal party also began to fish in troubled waters, and in 1919 pledged themselves to tariff reforms almost as drastic as those of the Progressives. The Conservative party alone remained true to the principles of adequate protection for all-a Canada first policy.
Owing to the three party system, the electors in 1921 put the Liberals, though a minority party, in power, and since their accession the tariff has been tinkered and tampered with, the hand of the Liberals being forced by the Progressives until nothing is certain in the business world but uncertainty. Following the precedent, of 1896 the Liberals increased the British preference with calamitous results to the woollen industry. In a single year 1923 Canada imported from Great Britain eleven and a half million yards of tweeds and worsteds, even more than the United States. The importation of woollen hose jumped from approximately two and three-quarter million pairs in 1921 to eight million pairs in 1923. It is significant to note here the effect that has had on the sheep industry in Canada. There are to-day from 750,000 to 1,000,000 less sheep in Canada than there were in 1921. Even such a staunch Liberal as Senator David has pro-

The Budget-Mr. Stinson
tested against this policy, which cuts directly at our own manufacturers. Then, with a wary eye to the farmers' vote, the duty on American agricultural machinery was reduced two and a half per cent, causing no reduction in price to the farmer but leading to an increase in imports of $3,716,000 and seriously damaging our steel industry. These reductions give new hope to the low tariff and free trade supporters, and the free trade movement has already increased in noise if not in strength. And now follow the motor reductions.
In view of these facts it is well worth our while to analyse carefully four aspects of the tariff problem:
1.	What has been the growth in Canada under protection?
2.	What is the relation of the present European situation to our industrial welfare?
3.	What is the position of the United States?
4.	Why should Canada not follow the example of Great Britain and pursue a free trade policy?
Now, as to the first problem, the development of Canada under protection. If the basic industries, agriculture, lumbering, mining and fishing have made remarkable progress, as well as the manufacturing industry; if the trade of Canada has enormously expanded, then we may reasonably draw the logical inference that protection has not hampered our advancement but has been a positive boon, keeping our raw materials for manufacture in Canada, creating new sources of wealth causing the appearance of factories backed by foreign capital, and making Canada a broader and more self-sufficient nation.
First of all let us note the remarkable development of our aggregate trade, which under protection has multiplied almost sixteen times. Our export trade climbed in 1922 to fifth place in the world as compared with tenth place in 1913. We are surpassed only by Great Britain, the United States, France and Germany. In 1922 we exported products valued at $100.63 per head of population, standing third in the world. In imports Canada stands eighth in the world. In 1879 our aggregate trade amounted to $149,488,188; in 1923 it had increased to $1,747,760,880. Our export trade with the United States in 1924 was $430,715,496, while in the same year we imported from the United States $601,295,121. Our trade with the British Empire increased, amounting to $414,163,218, of which $360,094,021 went to Great Britain in 1924. A noteworthy feature is the increased trade to the Orient, China buying $15,058,259 and Japan $25,696,621 in 1923.
The growth of agriculture in field crops between 1900 and 1923 is over five hundred per cent. Wheat production has increased three thousand per cent. The agricultural wealth of Canada in 1923 was $7,365,475,000. The agricultural revenue of Canada in 1923 was $1,342,132,000. Of that agricultural revenue Saskatchewan had $291,493,000, and Ontario $400,511,000. Ontario paid income taxes in 1923 to the amount of $25,435,613, whereas Saskatchewan paid $1,527,606. There was not much difference in the agricultural revenue, but as to taxation the large difference was paid by business, and yet our western friends would destroy it by their policy. If the Ontario farmers follow our western friends it will lead to their paying more taxes than they ever did before.
Now let me deal with other branches of industry. The lumbering industry between 1881 and 1922 increased over 300 per cent. The pulp and paper industry, a new industry fostered! by our tariff which comipels the most of our pulpwood to be manufactured in Canada, has a capital investment now of $381,006,000. Our fisheries, the finest in the world other than those of the North sea, have an annual production of $41,800,600 and have increased 600 per cent. The mining industry, in the period from 1881- to 1923, increased 210 per cent, and has a capital investment of $493,694,000. Our railways have increased in mileage 1,450 per cent. In the foregoing statistics I have covered the basic industries of agriculture, lumbering, mining and fishing.
Now let me come to manufacturing, which our friends from the west decry so much. The following figures will indicate the growth of this industry in the period from 1881 to 1921 inclusive:

In 1921 our exports to all countries amounted to $1,189,163,701. In 1924 our exports to all countries were $1,045,141,056, being less afteT the tinkering had taken place with the tariff. These figures bear silent and sure testimony to the increase in prosperity of Canada under a system of moderate protection. No branch of our life has failed to share in increased wealth, while on the other hand manufacturers have not excessively prospered at the expense of others. The fact that the average number of employees in a Canadian factory is less than twenty shows that protection, as is bo often charged, cannot have fostered monopolies and trusts to any appreciable degree, if at all. Furthermore, the tariff has been far from hampering the export of our primary
The Budget-Mr. Stinson

introducing the new tariff schedule, which gave substantial increases of duty on more than 50 items, Mr. Pratten, Minister for Trade and Customs, stated that within two years from 25,000 to 30,000 additional employees would be required for industrial development resulting from the new duties. Assuming that five persons were directly and indirectly dependent upon each wage-earner, from 100,000 to 150,000 persons would be advantaged. The new schedule reflected the desire of the Commonwealth government to assist industries which could be developed in Australia.
Meanwhile, the position of the primary producers of Australia is being steadily improved, not through tariff reductions which would be detrimental to industry, but through the introduction of better and more efficient marketing methods which tend to stabilize prices on a more profitable basis. A federal Department of Markets has been established, and according to the Prime Minister, the work of the new department "is giving satisfactory results in the orderly marketing of our primary products. The increasing production from our industries and the expansion of our overseas trade during the last decade is a wonderful record of achievement.
From many points of view textile and dothing factories provide the most interesting section of Australia's manufacturing industries. The doctrine that it has been an economic waste to send Australian wool to other countries and import manufactured goods made from that wool, instead of using the raw material locally and providing employment for a large number of Australians, has appealed to an increasing extent to the public mind of the commonwealth as ithe years have advanced. This point of view found expression in the recent changes made in the tariff, which have aJready had an important influence in improving the prospect of many mills and factories, and of stimulating greatly increased manufacture.
The effect of these tariff changes, plus trade depression and the reduced buying power of the farmer, has been very serious for the Canadian manufacturer. Between 1920 and 1922 the number of employees decreased from 685,349 to 517,144. Since then there has been some increase, but even now there are only 89 men employed in 1924 to 100 in 1920.
It is true that the tide of depression has already receded with Europe returning to normal, but competition for trade will be far heavier than in pre-war days. Belgium is ba/ck to pre-war production and hopes to expand. She has taken our glass trade. France has restored her devastated areas with the newest and most efficient equipment and has acquired the iron ores of Alsace-Lorraine and the coal of the Saar Valley. She is today the leading iron and coal country of Europe; she is almost entirely self-sufficient and potentially the richest country in Europe. Her greatest industrial problem is to secure sufficient labour without being swamped by foreigners. Italy has undergone a drastic purging and reorganization, will balance her budget in 1926 and is planning an intensive industrial campaign in order to absorb the labour of the large number of Italians now

barred from America. The German manufacturer, at ridiculously low cost, was able to wipe out his mortgages when the mark declined, and he modernized his plant. Concentration of industry has proceeded, then, by leaps and bounds. The German railways are now the best in Europe. Under the Dawes plan, accepted by the great powers, Germany will be paying heavy reparation sums for at least a decade to come. Fundamentally those reparations must be paid with goods, which means increased German production and increased export trade. As Herr Stresemann says:
The war caused the hot-house growth of manufactures -competition has grown much keener in 'the international market.
Austria is almost back to efficiency and is regaining her hold on Balkan trade, while Czechoslovakia is the best governed and least unharmed industrial country in Europe. Even Poland is settling down to peaceful ways. Mr Strachey, of the London Spectator, says:
Europe is at bottom in a thoroughly sound position-for trade reviv'all. It is full of skilful, eager workers, managers and traders of all sorts. It is also full of well-equipped factories and it has develop the scientific use of the various forms of power to a high degree of perfection.
In the light of these facts it can be seen that the Canadian manufacturer may scarcely hope to make any appreciable gain in export trade for some time to come. In fact, he will do well to retain his increased share gained during war time when Europe could not compete with him. He has certain prospects in the Orient but even there the German is fast becoming a powerful rival. One is more and more forced to the belief that the home market must be the great mainstay of the Canadian manufacturer, and the eastern farmer for years to come. If that market is destroyed for him by a low tariff or free trade his position will be exceedingly hazardous. We must see to it that such a tiling does not take place.
The second great factor in our tariff system is the United States, the colossus of the industrial world, with an area of unbounded fertility, of every variety of climate, with almost every resource for manufacturing except rubber and some of the minor metals and with a protection system established 135 years ago. The war gave her the supreme chance to seize world leadership in trade. She turned from a debtor to a creditor nation; she now possesses half of the world's gold and her wealth equals that of any other five nations combined. Her wealth was 350 billions in 1921, sixteen times our own. She possesses 45 per cent of the world's

Private Bills
iron and steel, 50 per cent of the coal, 60 per cent of the copper and cotton, 70 per cent of the oil. Through the war her manufacturing plants outgrew her home market and She is to-day the greatest exporting nation in the world. In 1922 her exportable surplus was 653 millions, an increase in nine years of 33j per cent.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
House rose at six o'clock I was pointing out some of the natural [DOT] difficulties we have to encounter owing to a decreased tariff. Geographically, Canada and the United States are one-the Maritime provinces looking to the New England states, British Columbia belonging to the Pacific, Ontario and Quebec sharing the Great Lakes system with the eastern states, and western Canada having the natural frontier. The resulting "pull" of the United States upon us, offering as she does superior wages and opportunities has been tremendous. Between 1921 and 1925 we lost in population to the United Spates some 500,000 people. Obviously with her wealth of population and her industrial machine American industry can in nearly every instance produce at a lower cost than can Canadian industry, and can offer a greater variety with her mass production. The effect is to be seen in our adverse trade balances with the United 'States. In 1901 our imports from the United States were $107,377,906. In the same year our exports to the United States were $67,983,673. Coming to the year 1923 we find that our imports from the United States were $540,917,432 and our exports to that country $369,0S0,218. In 1923 our imports from the United States formed 67 per cent of our total imports. The total import amounted to $60 per head of our population, while our exports to the United States amounted to $3.25 per head of her population.
The greater part of our imports from the United States are of manufactured articles, and the need of a tariff against her is obvious if we are to have any manufactures of importance and to become at all self-sufficient. Since the war the United States has seen fit to increase her tariff against us, especially against, our farm products, in order to protect her farmers. If a wealthy nation thinks protection advisable, we should have even more reason for adopting a similar policy. Moreover, protection compels the American manufacturer to establish branch factories in Canada, in order to share our trade. They employ Canadian workmen, and make investments in Canada which are of great value. Since 1901, six hundred and eleven American factories have come to Canada on account of protection, and nearly two and three-quarter billion dollars are invested in Canada. These factories represent 61 per cent of our motor industry, 40 per cent of our electrical apparatus, meat packing, rubber, brass and copper, condensed milk and petroleum industries. Without our tariff would these industries have come to Canada? I say no. Without increased protection shall we be able to attract

The Budget-Mr. Stinson
new firms or can we withstand American increased wealth and efficiency? Again I say no. The lower our tariff the fewer workmen we employ and the more of our sons we lose to the United States-a loss which we cannot replace and which we can least afford. The exodus from Canada during the last few years, especially the younger men, has been a great drain upon this country. We are losing some of our best brains to t'he United States, and this should not be allowed to take place.
Lastly our serious financial position makes it dangerous for us to run any risk of financial depression in industry through a low tariff. During the war we had to take over control of the Canadian National railways with 22,000 miles of track. These railways are built in excess of our present needs, they are heavily capitalized and have heavy interest charges to meet. Until 1923 they failed to meet operating expenses apart from interest charges. The annual fixed1 charges are nearly $70,000,000, if we include interest on loans and allowances made by the government. Despite the skill and energy of Sir Henry Thornton, we must face the prospect of a heavy burden in our railway system for years to come. If our industries are ruined by a low tariff the railways will be among the first to suffer, and their losses are the country's losses. If the industry of Ontario and Quebec be destroyed, the western freight rates must of necessity increase. If you take the report of the Canadian National Railway, you will find that the line is divided into three divisions, the eastern regional division, the central division and the western division, and of the three divisions the one that is making the profit is the central division, where you have the industrial population and industrial development. If that industrial development is ruined it means that the freight rates to the west must of necessity be increased. I acknowledge to our western friends that they cannot profit from protection to the same extent as we in the central provinces can. That being the case, so far as I am personally concerned I am willing to make amends to them in the matter of freight rates sufficient to take care of any additional amount that they lose by reason of protection.
The war has given Canada an increased debt of $2,453,776,869 as compared with $338,996,850 in 1914. The interest on our debt has increased from $14,687,796 to $136,007,667. Nearly two billion of that sum is war debt- an unproductive debt which added nothing to our resources. Furthermore we have not as yet reduced that debt one iota. On the contrary, when the railway financing is included,
it has increased. So long as that debt remains such a heavy charge, economy in government, coupled with increased production, is essential if we are to build up a surplus revenue. Our protective tariff represents a revenue of nearly $130,000,000. Reduce the tariff and that revenue falls. Can Canada afford that? Does the farmer want to pay the amount of tariff reduction in direct taxes? Our taxation is heavy enough, in all conscience-$43.15 per head as compared to $22.41 in 1913, or $5.88 in 1871. So far in discussing the tariff issue we have noted the progress made under protection in every branch of production, the growing dependence upon manufactures of our Canadian people, the increased competition in world trade caused by post-war conditions in Europe and America and the special need for stability, sound production and increasing revenue in order to meet our heavy burden of national debt. In view of these facts it is difficult to see how a low tariff is wise or justifiable.
There is one argument of the free trader, however, that has not yet been discussed. That is the argument by comparison, in which the theory is advanced that Great Britain has prospered as a free trade country and that Canada should do the same if she followed her example. By analysis of Britain's position that argument may be shattered. First of all, Britain only became a free trade country after centuries of protection during which she laid the foundation of her commercial and industrial strength. In the reign of Edward III, in the middle of the fifteenth century, England began to foster the weaving industry, to limit importation of goods and to discourage exports of raw materials. This policy was steadily pursued especially in Tudor times. Navigation acts in the seventeenth century fostered colonial trade and British shipping. At the close of the seventeenth century 1,200 imports were taxed. In the late eighteenth century, however, a series of inventions, coupled with abundant iron and coal and a long commercial experience, caused the famous industrial revolution which landed Britain on her career as the world's workshop. Europe was tom by wars and political unrest, the United States was a young struggling nation and Britain thus had the start by a half century. As Cobden and Bright boasted, Britain feared no competition at home and could undersell anybody abroad. Under these conditions Britain could well afford to relax protection, especially excessive duties on raw materials and food, since at that time agriculture was protected by the Corn Laws of 1815. Those laws particularly
The Budget-Mr. Stinson

affected the workers who were poorly paid and who were forced to pay high prices for food, and the manufacturer who wanted cheap raw materials, cheap food for his men and an increased exchange of manufactures from England for food in other countries. Then arose the campaign led by the middle class manufacturers for the repeal of the Com Laws. Subsequent to 1820 numerous duties were reduced; the Corn Laws disappeared between 1846 and 1860, and by 1860 virtual free trade existed. Hon. members will note that the transformation was spread over a period of forty years and took place only when Great Britain had a position of unsurpassed superiority.
The results of the movement are interesting. The repeal of the Com Laws led to a concentration on manufacturing and a onesided development of national life that made Britain dependent upon the world for seventy per cent of her food supplies. Her agricultural population fell from 49.8 per cent in 1846 to 21.9 per cent in 1913. In spite of such protection methods as her embargo upon Canadian cattle, only recently lifted, agriculture is one of the greatest problems of British life.
In the advancement of industry, while free trade has been her tariff policy, England has helped industry by such methods as the Trade Facilities Act, which affords ample capital for industrial concerns-surely an indirect form of protection; by discrimination in insurance risks against Canadian shipping, and other methods, and latterly by the Safeguarding of Industries Act.
To-day many in Britain seriously doubt whether she can afford to maintain free trade as her tariff policy. All parties are worried over British trade. The London Nation has opened its columns for a discussion of the conditions of British trade, while Labour admits that it cannot be a conjurer and sweep away unemployment at will. To-day Britain pays annually on her debt to United States a sum almost equal to her pre-war budget. She is beginning to wonder whether her present tariff policy is the safest one. She no longer leads the world in industry, being surpassed by the United States, while Germany and France are crowding on her heels. Even as matters stand she has an advantage over us in having no country such as the United States as a next-door neighbour and geographical twin.
We cannot, then, like Britain, accept free trade as our policy, because we have not the foundations of wealth and supremacy that Britain possessed when she accepted free trade; because our geographical position is

vastly different and because economic conditions have totally changed since that time. Viewing the matter from every angle we must admit that Canada must retain her policy of protection, that she cannot afford a low tariff as economic conditions are at present, and that the present uncertainty must be ended if Canadian industry and Canada itself are to prosper.
I read this afternoon a memorandum from the Premier of Australia showing conditions that had operated to their benefit by reason of their adopting a policy of manufacturing their wool in Australia rather than of shipping it abroad. Following that up it seems to me we should take a leaf out of her book in regard to our wheat. At the present time we are building up on Canadian wheat one of the greatest cities in the United States. The greatest milling centre in the world is Buffalo, and it has been built up there in the last few years largely upon Canadian wheat. Last year there was milled in the city of Buffalo something like 7,000,000 barrels of flour, while there was milled in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific some 19,000,000 barrels. They have adopted a system of milling in bond; in other words Canadian wheat can be shipped to Buffalo, milled in bond and sent out to compete in the world market with our Canadian flour. The result is that the United States is getting the direct benefit of that, is building up that wonderful city and at the same time taking away from us transportation charges that our railways need. If there was an export duty on Canadian wheat forcing the milling to take place in Canada, it would not in my opinion decrease or curtail our market, but it would add that further industry to Canada for both our labour and our railways.
This matter was referred to the royal inquiry commission and they made a report on it in which they stated that it was a matter of great importance not only to the millers of Canada but to the farmers of the country generally. I am going to read a short extract from the report as was made at that time:
At the present time, the duty on Canadian wheatentering the United States-is 42 cents per bushel. On wheat flour, crushed or cracked wheat, and similar wheat products, the duty is $1.04 per hundred pounds. These duties are practically prohibitive in their effect. They prevent Canadian wheat or wheat products having access to the American domestic market. On the other hand under the provisions governing milling-in-bond and drawbacks, it is quite possible for the American millers to obtain Canadian wheat virtually free of duty to grind for export. Considerable quantities of Canadian wheat are ground in American mills, and exported abroad under these conditions. This American flour ground in American mills, but the product of Cana-

The Budget-Mr. Stinson
dian wheat, enters into competition with the output of the Canadian flour mills. The benefits of manufacture are lost to Canada, while at the same time, the general benefits of reciprocal free trade in wheat and wheat flour do not exist. It was suggested to us that in view of these conditions, an export duty should be levied at the same rate as in thfe American tariff, upon Canadian wheat and wheat products entering the United States. The American tariff having already closed effectively the domestic market to the Canadian farmers, the result of such a levy would be to eliminate the export of American flour ground from Canadian wheat, and to transfer this market to the Canadian millers.
Now let us see for a moment how this milling in bond has been increasing. In 1921-22 the quantity of Canadian wheat milled in bond in United States was 6,172,837 bushels. In 1922-23 this had increased to 9,280,787 bushels, and in 1923-24 it had increased to 13,901,837 bushels. It will be noted that of the crop of 1923-24 the total reached the large quantity of over 13,900,000 bushels. The flour product of this quantity of wheat would be in excess of 3.000,000 barrels while the offal by-product would be 111,000 tons. These 3.000,000 barrels of flour made from straight Canadian wheat was sold abroad under United States trade names in direct competition with the product of Canadian mills. In the same twelve months Canada exported to countries other than the United States 11,973,916 barrels of flour.
Out of a total demand of 15,000,000 barrels of flour of Canadian quality, United States millers supplied no less than 20 per cent. With free Canadian wheat for this export trade, United States millers have certain advantages in rates 'and position which will always enable them to sell in competition with Canadian mills. Had the Canadian mills been in the competitive position natural and proper in view of all the conditions, then the extra 3,000,000 barrels should have been ground in Canadian mills and would have represented an increase of 25 per cent in export output. Now what does this mean to Canada? The manufacturer's costs of converting wheat into flour, including labour, selling expense and overhead, but not including the cost of bags or other containers, may be estimated at approximately sixty-five cents per barrel. At this rate the costs on 3,000,000 barrels would be $1,950,000. This amount was actually paid out in the United States in the year instead of being distributed to labour and capital in Canada. If Canada had milled this additional quantity Canadian transportation companies would have moved 14,000,000 bushels of wheat to Canadian mills and would have moved 3,000,000 barrels of flour and 111,000 tons of offal from Canadian mills, whereas this wheat actually moved direct by water from Fort 14011-190
William and Port Arthur to United States ports, chiefly in United States lake vessels, and no part of the product afterwards used Canadian routes. This meant that the loss to Canadian transportation companies on the movement of the wheat to the mills and the flour to the seaboard was in excess of $1,500,000. In addition to that, on the 111,000 tons of bran and shorts the additional earnings of Canadian transportation companies would have been 31 i cents per 100 pounds, or a total of 8679,300, if distributed for consumption in Canada, or a substantial portion of $550,000 if exported.
This movement of wheat to the United States is directly affecting a number of our own towns and cities in the matter of railway transportation. Take the town of Lindsay, which is a divisional centre on the Canadian National Railways. The wheat moved on the lakes and on Georgian bay to Midland passes through the towns of Lindsay and Belleville on its way to seaboard. But since this great milling industry 'has been established at Buffalo there has been a gradual falling off in the movement of wheat through Georgian bay to seaboard, with the result that the railway-men earned $200,000 less in wages in 1925 than in 1921 in the town of Lindsay. I am not attributing this fact entirely to the difference in the movement of grain, because certain other factors have to be taken into account; but in large measure it is due to the fact that the grain is going to Buffalo rather than through our own ports. It is time therefore that action were taken to remedy this condition of things. The grain should go through Canadian and not through American ports.
There is something else that must be considered.' Canada is losing all the advantage that would accrue from the sale of this flour under Canadian trade names. It is exported as United States domestic flour, 9 p.m. thus helping the United States to retain its reputation in the world's markets for high grade flour, to the benefit, whether blended or not, of all the domestic produce of that country. The effect on Canada is unfavourable. When selling, the United States miller may represent the flour as the product of Canadian wheat, or he may not. If he does not, the impression is created that perfect substitutes for Canadian wheat and flour can be found in another country, and that is absolutely to our detriment. The magnitude and importance of the Canadian milling industry are clearly shown by the official returns published in the latest issue of the Canada Year Book for the year 1922. The capital employed in 434 flour mills war

The Budget-Mr. Stinson

$65,928,521 and salaries and wages paid during the year totalled $7,083,398. The purchasing power of industry in the year, as represented by the amount paid out for material and supplies, was the very large sum of $125,312,923, and the value of the products, $151,237,671. The net difference between the latter two items, $25,924,748, represented the values created in Canada by the industry.
I realize that the prosperity of the Canadian farmer is fundamental to the development and success of the milling industry and wish it to be clearly understood that in advocating this duty I do so in the belief, not only that it would not depress prices, or restrict opportunities of sale for producers, but that on the other hand it would strengthen the position of Canadian products with advantage to every Canadian interest. If this flour were consumed in the United States, as it is not, that would mean that a market for Canadian wheat, which otherwise has been very limited and uncertain, would be enlarged by the use of wheat in this way. But under existing conditions no increase in the demand for Canadian wheat is brought about. If there is no increase in consumptive demand there can be no effect on the basis of prices. Indeed, the United States miller cannot be as substantial a support to the market as the Canadian miller, for the former can drop out of the business the moment he finds it equally profitable to grind United States wheat. The greater part of the milling in bond is done at Buffalo, but at any lake Erie port Canadian wheat can be laid down from Fort William-Port Arthur at a freight rate lower on the average than that to any Canadian port on the lakes. A mill at Buffalo pays lower transportation costs on Canadian wheat than does any eastern Canadian mill. It is by special laws and regulations of the government of the United States that the American miller has been put in a position to do this business. It is the policy of that government to give all the employment possible to United States labour and capital in its milling industry, even when the main product is not required in, and is even denied access to, the domestic market. As imports of Canadian wheat into the United States for actual consumption in that country are, under the present tariff, absolutely negligible and merely permit the export of a little more United States wheat or flour, in competition with Canadian products abroad, the general application of an export duty would not in such a case be open to objection on the ground that it might restrict the market for Canadian products.

I am deeply interested in Canada. I am interested in everything that will make Canada a nation worthy of her great natural resources, and I will support legislation that will bring that about, no matter what political party may introduce it. I should like to see Canada develop in such a way that we might have a job for every man at a reasonable wage so that he could maintain his home, educate his family and send them out fully equipped to take their place in the world. We want a Canada where the young Canadian can use his education and ability for the benefit of the land of his birth, and thus free his father and mother from the anguish of seeing him expatriate himself to a foreign country to make a living. We want a Canada-first policy, and that can be built up only upon a reasonable tariff system based upon scientific examination. That must be the settled policy of Canada. Tariff stability based upon protection is the greatest confidence builder known to business. It helps the farmer, the labourer, the manuacturer, the retailer; it assists and promotes evei-y branch of our national life.
Mr. CHAS. B. HOWARD (Sherbrooke): I rise to give my unqualified support to what is perhaps the most popular all-round budget that has ever been brought down in the Canadian parliament. I join with my leader in thankfulness that Canada which suffered so much during the Great war is one of the first of the allied countries to recover from the after-war depression. I also join with my friends on the other side of the House in "thanking Providence for having been so good to us". At the same time I like to think of the old maxim which was mentioned by my good friend from Lake St. John. (Mr. S.vlvestre) that "God helps those who help themselves".
Canada's great and increasing prosperity has been accomplished because all classes; the rich and the poor, the mighty and the weak, the capitalist and the labourer, regardless of race or religion, have joined together in this commendable work. The common people have placed their shoulders to the wheel, and guided by a sane government, have accomplished world-renowned achievements! I was pleased the other day to listen to the speech of one of the oldest members of this House, my hon. friend from Bona venture (Mr. Marcil), who did not hesitate to say that the present budget was the finest of any that he had listened to during his twenty-seven years as a member of this House. Twenty-seven yean takes us back to the days when Sir Wilfrid

77ie Budget-Mr. Howard
Laurier was in power and when the national ddbt was at its minimum, and consequently taxation was light and any increase of taxes did not affect the people so directly as it would at the present time, particularly as any increase then naturally followed the steady development of the country. But during t'he ten years from 1911 to 1921, our national debt was increased by $2,000,000,000. as we say in French; parce qu'ils avaient tous les mains dans le plat; and therefore our rejoicing today is all the greater that the Minister of Finance has been able to bring down a budget containing a substantial reduction of taxation. I am pleased to be a member of the House in this fifteenth parliament because I believe that in the years to come this budget will be regarded as one of the greatest achievements in our political history and will be looked back upon as one of the milestones in Canadian development.
I pick up the local paper from mv home town and on the front page in big headlines I read this:
British budget is presented by the Hon. Churchill. General trade improving, but basic industries depressed.
J present this by way of comparison after listening to my hon. friend on the other side (Mr. Stinson) who stated in his speech that the basic industries of Canada were improving. The next statement is this:
Under budget as presented existing rate of taxation will be continued for 1926-27.
England, the Mother of Parliaments, and her taxation rate for 1926-27 is to be continued on the same basis! Contrast this with the budget of Canada-notre pays-substantially reducing taxation so soon after the war. There is no question about our increasing prosperity. Money in the pockets of the people will show that business is improving. But in case my statement should be doubted, let me cite two items which it has been a great pleasure for me to read recently. One is:
The Canadian Pacific Railway March net best since 1918. Gross up $1,300,000 over March 1925, while expenses increased only $623,306. Good first quarter. Net $2,675,000 above that shown in first quarter of last year.
In other words, the net for the first quarter of the year of that transportation system of which we are all so justly proud shows an increase of $2,675,000. Then we are also pleased that the Canadian National Railways-our own system-for the month of March comes out with these figures:
A net of $4,191,000, an increase of $2,500,000 over the same period last year, or an increase of 156 per cent.
Now, these reports coming from our two great railway systems are significant. Taking 14011-190i
the Canadian National figures, if you multiply the $2,500,000 by twelve, I think you will see that by the end of this year the system will be able to meet its interest to the public.

speechtext:
I would ask hon. members to listen to this evidence of prosperity in the business world:
The Ford output at the Canadian plant is still growing, there being an increase of over 8,000 cars in the five month period compared with a similar period last year. The output of tractors is also on the increase.
This is not a statement given out for the government, but a statement furnished to the company's shareholders. At the bottom I find the following:
The total sales and income for the five month period is $16,191,000, an increase of over $5,000,000 in the first five months over last year. Showing a net profit of $1,000,000 for the period.
Let me give another item concerning the automobile industry generally:
"The auto industry attains a record output for 1925." There were manufactured in Canada during 1925, 124,000 cars, worth $82,000,000. . . . export shipments from Canada were the highest on record, the total value of automobiles and parts exported during the year being $39,000,000.
One more item to show our increasing prosperity. This is from the banking standpoint, and it comes very near to me, for it is published in the Financial Times, and we know the politics of this paper. It states in connection with the building of a new paper mill just north of the city of Sherbrooke:
About five years ago this same company was Obliged to put out a bond issue carrying a rate of interest of 8 per cent, and it sold just as few bonds as it possibly could. When it is ready to build its new paper mill,
The Budget-Mr. Howard

instead of re-financing, the president says: "We have arranged with our bank to loan us the money by our putting up these 8 per cent bonds as collateral security and getting our money at 6 per cent."
This shows the improved financial situation in the banking and industrial world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what I think we should ask ourselves in connection with the budget is this:	Was this reduction in taxation justified? In replying to that question, lest my figures may be disputed by some hon. members on the other side, as they have just been disputed by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), instead of taking my figures from the Canada Year Book or the blue books of this government I will take them from the 1925 report of the Royal Bank of Canada. I take that report because I see from its first page that the president of that institution is one of the head Tories of Canada, so I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite will not dispute these figures. There are no figures given for 1911, but at page 26 of that report I find that in 1910 the net public debt of Canada was $48.64 per capita, and that in 1921, when this government came back into power, the net debt per capita was $266.36; in other words, it had jumped from $48.64 to $266.36. The next year there was an increase of $4. Then what do I find? In 1925 it had decreased to $258.16, a decrease of $8.20 per capita for every person in Canada.
Turning to the next page of the report, page 27, I find that the total gross debt of Canada w'as practically the same in the years 1923 and 1924, but in 1925 it had decreased by $80,000,000. I also find that the net debt in 1923 was $1,814,000 000, and in 1921, $1,804,000,000, or a decrease of $10,000,000. In 1925, the net debt of Canada was $1,767,000,000, a further decrease of $37,000,000, which, with the $10,000,000 decrease of the previous year makes for the two years a decrease, according to Conservative figures, of $47,000,000. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this justifies the reduction which this budget proposes in the present income tax.

It has been stated in practically all the Tory press during the past two weeks that every member on the Liberal side and on the Progressive side of this House discusses only the reduction in the automobile tax. I would like you to remember, Mr. Speaker, that this income tax was put in force in 1917 and became effective on the 1st of April, 1918, and I have no hesitation in saying to this House that the system of income taxation as called for under the income tax legislation of 1918 was one of the rottenest systems that has ever been put over any country. I say so because it disregarded the fact that all people in this country have the same rights. The government of that day placed upon the statute book that famous surtax, and anybody who knows what a surtax is knows that it is simply a way of allowing the rich man to get a preference over the man who is earning an ordinary salary. I am proud to stand on this side of the House and to say that under the income tax proposals brought down by the present Minister of Finance there is no class distinction of any kind. I also wish to state that the load has been lightened especially for those people who needed relief, the man whose salary was reported by his employer, and who perhaps was raising the large or the largest family, and therefore needed the most relief. This government has seen fit to raise the exemption of that class.
About two days after this budget was brought down, somebody ran across a certain kind of income that might bear a heavier tax than in the previous year. The Tory press broadcast the fact that the income tax reduction was only a bluff, that as a matter of fact there was an increase in the tax. There can be no question about the $3,000 exemption, but let us take the business man who is carrying the load of the country and has an income of, say, $10,000. Last year the man with an income of $10,000 paid $619.50; this year he will pay $290. One thing more. Travelling up and down this country in the last five years I have come across this situation, which has been remedied by this budget. A man will ask you on the train:	Who makes up your income tax? Naturally you will mention whoever is your auditor in your home town, and then he will say to you: "I used to be employed with the Income Tax department, but I am now in business for myself; if you will allow me to make up your income tax I will save you one-half of what you are paying now and we will go fifty-fifty on the balance." The Tory press call this a Progressive budget. I would like to ask them how they get that way. There is not one single Progressive member from the province of Quebec, and yet there is not a member from that province who does not support every clause of this budget. If this budget was dictated by the Progressives, how do you account for the cut in the rich man's income tax? I go further: I say that this budget was brought down by the Liberal party with the help of the Progressive party, because they are willing to assist in the passing of any legislation which is in the best interests of the people of Canada as a whole. There have been many governments with a majority running from thirty to fifty in this House who would never have dared to face the financial interests of Canada and bring down a budget favourable to all classes, but this government, which on the first vote taken in this House had a majority of only three, and which, with our allies the Progressives, has a majority to-day running from only ten to fifteen, were not
afraid to take the consequences. We stand, therefore, on the merits of this budget.
We have been criticized by our Tory friends and the Tory papers on the ground that Canadian industries are hurt by this budget. I should like those who really think that is the case to turn to page 2456 of Hansard and in the part of the budget recorded there they will see whether this government stands by Canadian industries or not. An industry in the town of Drummondville which is spending $7,000,000 to-day on the erection of one of the finest cellulose manufacturing plants in Canada, came to this government and received what? They were allowed to bring in from the United States a certain part of the material they required for one year practically free of duty, and another part of the material for two years, so that they could get their own plant going by that time. When their own plant is in operation the tariff will be applicable as it is to-day.
With respect to the argument that this budget will discourage Canadian industries let me point out that the Montreal Gazette of yesterday states that the Spruce Falls Power and Paper Company's industry will be developed at a cost of $25,000,000. That industry is in the province of Ontario. Now that industry is not afraid to spend $25,000,000 just after the bringing down of the budget. But I want to tell hon. gentlemen of the prosperity that is coming to the province of Quebec. Perhaps it is not generally known that the Aluminum Company of America is spending in the northern part of that province the enormous sum of $100,000,000, two and a half times the totali valuation of the city which did me the honour to send me here. One development involving an expenditure of $100,000,000! And those people are coming here and are going to manufacture aluminum in the face of the budget brought down on April 15 last.
I do not desire to criticize the budget in any way, but I should like to see the time soon when the stamps on notes will be the same as on cheques, and I feel sure this will be realized in due course. I should like also to see the restoration of the duty that was taken off cyanide pumps in 1914 by the Tory government, thus allowing them to be manufactured in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and shipped to t'he great mining companies in northern Ontario and northern Quebec free of duty. Whatever that duty was I should like to see it restored, so that the business of $50,000 which went out of Canada last year will go to the city of Sherbrooke. I say that not because I want the price to be increased.

but because I think Canada is entitled to that business. I congratulate t'he government on keeping out inferior spring scales such as might cheat the Canadian consumer.
Now I come to the tariff on automobiles. I wish to be perfectly frank in my statement. Most of you know my position on the tariff question, but I will state it again. I believe in using the tariff to protect our industr;es, to protect our farmers, and to protect our consumers as long as that protection is not taken advantage of to increase the price unduly. I believe in using the tariff to eliminate foreign competition-

-but I do not believe in allowing any monopoly to start in this country, keeping it on the nursing bottle for over twenty years, and then allowing it to bleed the Canadian consumer without taking any steps to reduce the price. The hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) stated the other night that the tariff would not increase the price of articles. If he were here to-night I would ask him how he could make such a statement as that in view of the price of Canadian automobiles as compared with the price of American automobiles? To illustrate my point with respect to the effect of the duty, let me say that in Sherbrooke we have an industry employing five hundred hands. There is a duty on the class of goods which it makes of twenty-seven and a half per cent. But the Canadian price to the Canadian consumer instead of being higher than the American price to the American consumer is actually less. There is another industry in Sherbrooke engaged in another line of manufacturing, which enjoys a protection of thirty-five per cent, the same as the manufacturers of automobiles had. Yet that factory's price in Sherbrooke to the Canadian consumer is exactly the same as the price for the same line of goods in the United States. There is not a member in this House who does not know that the Canadian workman

The Budget-Mr. Howard
is the finest workman in the world, bar none We want to do everything we can to protect him, but I ask hon. gentlemen to be honest and fair. Industries that were in the business during the war, employing 4,000 to 6,000 men, did not close their doors the morning after the Armistice was signed in November, 1918. They did not put their workmen at once on the streets, but kept them for months afterwards; they did not remove them until the country could absorb the surplus labour. That is why I say-and I believe it is the opinion of the people of Canada generally- that any firm who would close their doors and put their faithful employees on the street before knowing what the effect of the budget on the people of Canada would be, have no right to manufacture in this country. If the manufacturers had been honest and played the game fairly, no government, neither this government nor any other, would want to do anything to injure the industry, because we all should have but one aim, the upbuilding of our country.
Some feeling has been expressed, some suggestions have been thrown out and statements made, that this was a movement of the province of Quebec against Ontario. I deprecate such remarks as these. Anything that benefits Ontario benefits Quebec, and anything that benefits Quebec benefits Ontario. I will give you one example to-night to show whether or not Quebec is playing fairly. The Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company is paying to this country, an income tax of three-quarters of a million dollars and is supplying power to the citizens of the province of Quebec in the district of Montreal, while the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission, which is supplying citizens around Toronto, is not paying one nickel by way of income tax. We in Quebec think they should be on the same basis as our Quebec companies. When we talk about justice in this country we mean justice to everybody, rich and poor, the people in the west and those in the Maritime provinces, and as long as the present government remains in power this country can be assured that they will rceeive even-handed justice.
In the United States there is one automobile to every six people. In Canada there is only one automobile to every thirteen people. When an automobile manufacturer tells you that he will close up his factory in Canada and go back to the United States he knows he is bluffing. He knows that this country of ours, Canada, which our taxpayers have built up, is the only country in the world where he can build a car, get the advantage of the British preference and sell it
in the British Empire, which extends round the whole globe. The automobile manufacturer knows that the Australian government demands that in order to obtain the benefit of the British preference he has to make 50 per cent of his car in Canada, and that is where the rub comes. He wants to get the benefit of the British preference if ten per cent is manufactured in Canada. He also knows that in one of the small British possessions, India, there are three hundred million people; they are only beginning to build their highways, and they will be the greatest purchaser of automobiles in the future. For my part I want to do justice to the automobile manufacturers. We want to treat them fairly but we should see that they treat the Canadian purchaser accordingly. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), stated he would apply the golden rule. In other words, we should treat them the same as they treat us-meaning the United States. A book was handed to me by the Minister of Finance which showed that you could'manufacture automobiles in Canada and ship them to the United States on the payment of 25 per cent duty. But when you make them in the United States and bring them in Canada there is a duty of 35 per cent. My hon. friend must have forgotten that in advocating his polic}' of brick for brick!
The hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) following the speech of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) the other night, directed a question to me, namely, he asked me how I liked the tariff policy which the hon. member for St. Boniface has expounded. I leave it to the House to say whether there is any difference between the policy I have enunciated to-night and the policy expressed by the hon. member for St. Boniface. He spoke about the duty on vegetables coming into Canada, the duty on potatoes, strawberries and so forth. We have a tariff board, and my opinion on this subject is that there is no need to place a duty on those products from the month of January to the month of July when Canada does not produce any of them. But if the tariff board adjudges that these products during the season they are produced in Canada are subjected to foreign competition, it is for them to decide whether they should put on a duty to eliminate that foreign competition. The matter has already been submitted to them.
In conclusion, as I see the situation it amounts to this: when this House convened on January 7, the present government was

The Budget-Mr. Howard
sustained by a majority of three. This government asked for an adjournment of six weeks in order to elect their ministers in the best interests of Canada. But that adjournment was held off and was cancelled by the action of members of the opposition. If they had granted that adjournment, they might have reduced that majority by one, but they did not do so and consequently the majority is increasing every day and has increased. I sat in this House and heard the speech delivered by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) when he spoke for about three hours:-one of the greatest addresses that has ever been delivered in this chamber-on the eve of the election in Prince Albert. It was supposed to have been in the interest of Canada, but I have decided that it was in the interest of the Conservative party. The result of the Customs investigation, which we cannot speak of in this House until the report from that committee comes in, will justify my remarks in due course. But up to date there has not been one particle of suggestive criticism offered.
In closing I am frank to state that all that is the matter with the opposition and their discussion on this question is the fact that they regret that their lack of tactics and generalship has increased our majorities and has placed the present government in power for years to come and prevented the opposition from bringing down this very same budget 1
