speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg the indulgence of this House for a time, I hope not too long to-night, to offer my support to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) to the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). There has been a good deal of discussion in this House over the budget and no doubt a great deal of interest is being taken in it throughout the whole Dominion of Canada. This interest is well justified because it constitutes the business programme of the country for the coming year.
Some have termed it an "election" budget. If it is it may still serve for better government. Others term it a "Saskatchewan" budget, and as hon. members from that province smile almost in jubilation at the most contentious changes it enunciates, one cannot help thinking that the desires long since expressed by the three ministers from Saskatchewan on fiscal matters are being more and more felt by the government. It has also been termed,
I believe, by the hon. member for Fort William as an "American" budget, and I fear

if its principles are put into effect that such a description may be justified. As I listened, however, to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), independent though lhe professes to foe, enthusiastically defend it in detail, and with apparent satisfaction endorse it in full and laud the government in general, I wondered if it would be fair to term it a "Forke-handled" budget. Whether or not there is in any of these terms a proper description the government alone ' may know, but surely such a budget would have been indescribable to themselves at the time when the Speech from the Throne was brought down in this House, when parliament and the people in general were solemnly promised that no change in the fiscal policy of the country would foe made without a thorough investigation by the tariff commission into the affaire of the industries concerned. Since then the tariff commission, which was appointed in due time, was expected to assume the responsibilities for which it was created, namely, to investigate such industries.
I cannot say whether the automobile industry has been unduly protected or not or whether this is too great a reduction in the tariff or not enough. If this government assume to know, why appoint a tariff board? If they do not know, why speculate so recklessly with a theory that practically threatens the existence of a great and growing industry? It is surely reasonable to assume that an industry involving 180,000,000 of capital investment in this country, employing 20,000 skilled labourers with a payroll of over $30,000,000 annually and supporting 100,000 people who are directly interested, would be worthy of the consideration of this new board if its appointment is in any way going to be justified by this government. The action of the government seems as if it realized the futility of the board to act effectively without any principle by which to function. If that should be the reason for our not having a report from this new tariff eommisison, this reduction in the duty of 15 per cent, or a reduction of 43 per cent of the original protection on automobiles by the government will at least serve as an enlightenment of the principle on which the government desires the new board to function with reference to the boot and shoe industry, the furniture industry, the silk industry and other industrial enterprises that enjoy similar protection.
The hon. member for Brandon has on different occasions explained his unselfishness, stating that sectional desires are far from his mind. As a farmer I might be pardoned if I too give expression to my own unselfishness as to these tariff changes, as I rep-

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
resent the riding of Dufferin-Simcoe which has not a manufacturing plant in any way subsidiary to the manufacture of automobiles, but which is a large rural riding almost solely engaged in agriculture for which its fertile soil is favourably adapted, and therefore which is a riding of purchasers of motor cars and other machinery manufactured outside of the riding. I feel that if I were to admit any selfishness it would certainly not be with any lack of interest in the agriculturists of Canada. When I say "agriculturists" I do not mean only those who are engaged in one phase of that great enterprise, but I am also mindful of those engaged in mixed farming who make up by far the greater majority of the agricultural class in Canada to-day.
The reason, that I am here to-day is because the agriculturists of my riding realize that a national protective policy as enunciated by the leader of the Conservative party is of fundamental importance to their interests. Therefore I wish to make it clear to this House that even though the hon. member for Brandon leads a remnant of what once promised to be an important party in this country and though he has a special circumstantial influence in this parliament which he may never enjoy in the same way again, he in no way represents the farmers in Canada outside of a very few sections when he states that the farmers do not want protection and that a home market is not of fundamental importance to the future success of our business.
I do not want to reflect in any way or. the sincerity of my hon. friends to the left when they say that they are not a class or a sectional representation in this House because I feel that they are sincere in their interest in the whole welfare of our Canadian people. But I regret that such a reference to their sincerity of purpose is in no way a tribute to their judgment of practice in the interest of agriculture because I feel that the interests of industry and agriculture in Canada are so closely identified that any fiscal policy that retards in any way one of these great basic industries, similarly reflects on the other. I realize that at this particular time in our country's history wheatgrowing does not feel the benefit of a protective policy to the same extent that the balance of agricultural production does and while I hope I realize fully the value of wheat production in agriculture, I also realize that no matter how fertile any soil may be, it cannot be used indefinitely for the production of wheat alone, so that Canada is already fast becoming a country of mixed farming.
We saw long ago the effects of lowering the duties to benefit one particular class in this country, and the results invariably were such as were experienced in the lowering of duties on farm implements. This did not benefit the farmers one dollar; in fact, after that reduction by this government they paid more for almost every tool of production which they used on their farms, and other classes suffered and were forced to deplete the home market by going to a foreign market to manufacture the implements there. We have watched our Canadian people leave our country to seek employment since this government came into power. There are 15,000 Canadians engaged in the farm tractor industry in the United States who ought to be working in this country. What we need is a policy that will keep these people employed in Canada, preserve to them a high standard of living, and increase the home market for all our agricultural producers, as well as for our manufacturers and retailers. Such a policy is bound to react favourably upon those who are engaged professionally and upon all other classes of the community.
It is not necessary to put on Hansard facts and figures which probably are already on record. It would seem, however, that the government at any rate has not yet realized the situation in Canada sufficiently to see the error of its ways. We know what the effect of its policy has been on the fertilizer industry as well as on farm implements. The result of their theorizing has been to put out of business a large portion of our fertilizer manufacturing industry. This has depleted the market for farm products in Canada by driving out of the country, to seek employment in the United States and elsewhere, those workmen who were engaged in this industry. And far from the government's efforts resulting in a lowering of the price of fertilizer it has increased it: the American manufacturer is now able to charge higher prices because of less Canadian competition.
Some Canadians may be satisfied to remain just producers of wheat and the recipients of the surplus industrial products of the United States. But is it fair that, because they happen to hold that innocent international view, this country should give to the American, the Australian and the New Zealand agriculturist, as it does to-day, an advantage over the Canadian farmer in eggs, butter, cheese, meats, grains, fruits and in fact every other commodity for which the home market is badly needed? I need not put on Hansard the list of duties, which I
The Budget-Mr. Rowe

fancj' has already been reported, but why should we allow, almost $200,000,000 worth of foreign agricultural products to be sold in Canada under an advantageous tariff? The wheat producer of Canada prays that Europeans may continue to eat white bread in order to take his surplus, and he wants special transportation rates. He is not concerned with the home market. But he seems to forget that after all wheat growing is only one phase of a great enterprise in a district in which, unless all natural precedents fail, there will be a more diversified production before long. If only the Canadian market were protected for the Canadian farmer there are many lines of agriculture which would prove just as profitable as the growing of wheat. Under a proper system of protection, not only would our home market be enlarged, but important phases of agricultural endeavour would be directly stimulated, as for example, the textile industry. Surely this government should have studiously avoided the error committed by its own party under its great chieftain, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who, realizing the disastrous effect upon eighty-eight woollen textile mills after the lowering of the duty in 1897, retrieved his mistake and increased the tariff again from 23J to 30 per cent in 1904. Is it not a strange fact that before 1900 we had more sheep in Canada than we have to-day? In 1921, before the present government speculated in freer trade and lowered the duty on textiles, we had 1,000,000 sheep more than we have now. Our textile industry suffered heavy losses and thousands were put out of employment, being forced to leave their homes. Previous to that time we had 3,600,000 sheep and lambs, as against 2,500,000 to-day. Canada is by climate adapted to the raising of sheep, and with our vast areas we have only 2,500,000 as compared with 25,000,000 in England, with its small territory. And Australia has 80,000,000 head. With the aid of the so-called farmer party this government saw fit to reduce the duty on Australian mutton from three cents to one-half cent, allowing that dominion a special advantage also in woollen products. Since the British preference was lowered we find that almost one-half of the total imports from Great Britain have been textile products, which in 1925 amounted to over $72,000,000. Is this fair to the Canadian textile industry?
In 1923 the present government, through the French treaty, reduced our duty on French textiles to nineteen per cent on some lines, and below 30 per cent on all. Although Great Britain, still believed by some to be a 
free trade country, protects its textile manufacturers to the extent of 33 J per cent against competition, the idustry in that country pays less in wages to its factory hands than do the Canadian mills. Since 1923 our imports of woollen and knitted goods from France have increased three-fold, until in 1925 they amounted to over $3,000,000. When we consider that we produce only one-half of the textile requirements of our people and that the farmers produce only one-fifth of the raw wool consumed in Canada, is there any justification whatever for any action that tends to discourage such a great dual enterprise as the woollen industry? As a producer of mutton and wool I claim that with adequate protection for our textile industry, as well as protection against foreign mutton and raw wool, we might increase our sheep industry by one hundred per cent, with considerable advantage to this Dominion. The sheep industry is one that increases the fertility and productive qualities of the soil instead of robbing it of its best elements, as the growing of wheat tends inevitably to do.
When I say, Mr. Speaker, that a sound protective policy is as essential to argicultural development as it is to industry, I think I am only voicing the opinion of our party, as enunciated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) in his resolution of a year ago, that we should protect the products of Canadian agriculture against- unfair competition from foreign commodities which enjoy a tariff advantage. This particular phase of a national protective policy is recognized as most essential to the agricultural area of Dufferin-Simcoe which I represent. But realizing that a policy of national protection is bound to reflect its advantages in every locality, I would not consider it fair if I did not advocate, equally in the case of other activities, the same principle of adequate protection. I believe in the principle of protection as applied not only to the enterprises of my own constituency, but to coal and steel in the east, and industrial enterprises, just as I view with sympathy the question of western freight rates. My ideal is a policy that will make for national development throughout the Dominion as a whole.
I want to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhbb) on the picture he has painted in his budget of the improved conditions of the country at the present time No doubt he had the advantage of the blesset co-operation of Providence-; nature smiling or. our wheat fields during the past year provided a good background for that picture. I

The Budget-Mr. Fansher
have no doubt the reductions in the income tax and the stamp tax will be welcomed, even if they do seem to be a couple of years late in coming. It would appear that the sales tax, the receipt tax and the tax on cheques, all increased by this government when it came into power, might well have been materially reduced if not abolished. Since the present government took office in 1921 the tax collections have been greater year by year than they were in any year of the former government.
Now, independent of the bright and picturesque appearance of the budget, we find that last year's expenditure was some $22,300,000 over previous years, and our estimates for the coming year promise still greater expenditure. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while the government seem to have become artists in the painless extraction of taxes from our people, it would be more economically sound if, first, they would show a reduction of expenditure; then the other side of the ledger might be expected to follow favourably, as a natural consequence.
It is indeed gratifying to anyone in public life to note the great respect that the mem-oers of the different parties have in common for the traditions and lives of those two great leaders, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the late Sir John A Macdonald, but I am sure the country resets that there is no evidence in the present government of a desire to perpetuate the policy of their late great leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, whose traditions of stable government have been forgotten, or exchanged for the good-will of the Progressive party in order that the government may continue to enjoy administrative power.
The hon. member for Brandon, (Mr. Forke), who was at one time hailed as a farmer leader, according to a press report, stated in Toronto that he had been termed a Liberal, but that he was not, that he was only a Liberal in action, or an "advanced Liberal". If he is correctly reported, he no doubt was talking true to form by classifying himself as nearly to the Liberal party as words could classify him, and the only, evidence of any greater similarity would be his votes and utterances in parliament. His words, Mr. Speaker, were surely carefully selected, because it seems rather unique that in order apparently to secure the support of himself and his party the government might well be classified as "advanced Liberals," they having never hesitated to break any advanced promises they have made in order to allow the hon. member for Brandon and his friends to be "Liberals in action." For some time I have
been much interested in the hon. leader of the Progressive party. He follows the same vocation as I do, and he was at one time supposed to represent that particular class of our people in parliament. But the large and expansive agricultural area that has constituted his environment no doubt tended to broaden his views. Therefore it is not any wonder to-day that the people of Canada can scarcely perceive whether the one time Farmer party has broadened from its earlier class consciousness and absorbed the Liberal party, or whether the Liberal party has broadened from its identity with great traditions and absorbed the Progressive party, or whether both parties,, as David said of his enemies, "have covered themselves with their own confusion." Perhaps so far as the interests of Canada are concerned that matters not; but one thing they have done-they have covered industry and labour with a confusion of dissatisfaction, uncertainty and lack of confidence that will reflect on many lines of enterprise and possible development in this country.
Is it not time, therefore, that we had some stability in our fiscal policy in the interests of commercial, industrial and agricultural advancement in this favoured land of great resources and possibilities? Is it not also time that we had some stability in government policy to restore confidence in a great and energetic people who await Canadian opportunities for a high standard of living in preference to the hope of employment in a foreign country?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this is the first occasion of my addressing this House I crave your indulgence while I make a few observations on the budget. Before doing so I wish to draw attention to a few remarks made by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Stinson) with reference to the milling of wheat in Canada. He quoted a recommendation in the report of the grain inquiry commission, which was appointed to investigate the grain trade from A to Z, that an embargo of 42 cents per bushel be placed on wheat going to the United States. I have a memorandum here which shows that the average price of Canadian flour on the Liverpool market for the month of March was 381 cents per sack lower than the price for the same quality of Canadian flour in Winnipeg. If we add the 42 cent6 duty, or the embargo, to that 381 cents, we would be paying 801 cents more for our sack of flour in western Canada than the Liverpool consumer would have to pay.
The Budget-Mr. Fansher

The hon. member for Dufferin-SimcoefMr. Rowe), who has just sat down, has told us how the farm implement business has gone to pieces in the last few years, particularly since the election of 1921, I am sorry I have not the exact figures before me, but they have been placed on Hansard, and if my memory serves me correctly they show that there are considerably more than one thousand more men employed in that industry now than four years ago.
He also made reference to the textile industry, and argued for protection for that industry. It is amply protected now, I think, to enable it to stand on its own feet. I would just like to remark here, dealing with it more fully a little later on, that any* business that is running efficiently must of necessity manufacture as cheaply as possible. It must get its raw material as cheaply as possible, and must cut out all waste and all non-essentials if it is to compete in the world's markets with other industries of the same character. We are producing what we can produce in Canada more cheaply than other countries. We are doing it 'sometimes under a handicap of weather, sometimes under a handicap of other conditions, but always under the handicap of protective tariffs. While we export many millions of dollars' worth of the products of this country, we have to import a similar amount of other articles that we do not produce, or cannot produce as cheaply, in Canada, and if you inquire into the textile industry in detail you will find that that is the reason why the textile industry in this country is suffering to some extent, and especially does that apply to the cotton industries.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe was very solicitous for the welfare of the Progressive party. I do not wish to take up his remarks in a critical spirit, but if he continues to speak in the same tone of the Progressive party I should just like to suggest that he may find himself in a year or two in the position described by these lines:
Vice is a monster of so frightful mien,
As to be hated needs but to be seen;
Aet seen too oft, familiar with her face,
We first endure, then pity, then embrace.
In another year or two we shall possibly see him embracing the principles of the Progressive party.
I should like to speak for a moment of the beneficial effect the principle involved in this budget will have upon business in general throughout Canada. It is very pleasant, I am sure, to the entire population of this fair Dominion to know that we have at last come to the point where we can meet our expenditure from current revenue, and have

a tidy sum left over to our credit. Some few years ago in western Canada, and I have the privilege of representing a western constituency, we almost despaired that that time would ever come, but here we are. We have reduced our national debt, not by a large amount it is true, but still very appreciably considering the years through which we have come. It is also very gratifying to know that the Canadian National Railway is almost at a point now where it will no longer be a drain upon the Dominion treasury. We are sure that the managing general, so to speak, of that great railroad, will soon bring it to the point where it will be paying back large sums every year of the money that has been advanced.
I think all will agree with me that the great basic industry of Canada is agriculture. I do not need to argue that point, or to bring any proofs, because it is generally admitted. We have been told for a number of years at election time, we have been told on the floor of this House, and we have been told through the press of this country, that agriculture is our great basic industry, the foundation of all other industries. The reports of all the Canadian banks in the past year bear out mj contention. Agriculture is our great bask industry; it produces an enormous amount oi wealth, and because of the new wealth it brings into the country it has 'a beneficial effect on all other industries in Canada that cannot be gainsaid. The agricultural production of this country has contributed to the exports of Canada to the extent of 82 per cent, and an industry contributing such a large percentage to the wealth of Canada surely deserves, consideration. But agriculture has been in distress for some time. I am sure that when I have finished my remarks hon. gentlemen will see that it is necessary to relieve this industry from that distress, in order that other industries may enjoy what they would like to enjoy through protection.
Through protection the whole cost of living is gradually raised to a higher level. The man in the factory has to pay more for his clothes, for his furniture, for everything that he consumes. Therefore, he has to get more wages. That increase in wages has to be added to the cost of the article that he produces, and so the merry circle goes, until we have built up a cost of production in Canada that will not enable us to compete with other countries in the world's markets. There is another thing that has added very materially to this cost of production of which I shall speak a little later, but I wish to say here

The Budget-Mr. Fansher
that the principle involved in this budget, namely, that of lowering the duties, is a step in the right direction which will gradually lower the cost of production so that we can successfully compete with other countries in the world's markets.
I would suggest that in the next budget submitted to this parliament there be a reduction in the duties on the necessities of life. That would be of advantage to everyone throughout Canada, and would tend to lower the cost of production of which I have just spoken. We have- heard a good deal about the loss of population in Canada, about our young men and young women crossing the international boundary line to get work. The situation seems to me to resolve itself into a fight, as it were; a competition between the industrial part and the agricultural part of Canada, or between other industries and the great basic industry of agriculture. A certain pressure has been exerted against this great basic industry that it has not been able to stand, and it has been crumbling. Coming from western Canada I know whereof I speak. Many a farmer in consequence of this pressure has gone to the wall and has crossed to the United States, and in some cases has been assisted to go there. In other instances the farmer has saved enough out of the wreck to enable him to go to the United States without assistance in order to get work. This has been the result of the crumbling process I speak of which has been in operation for a number of years and was largely brought about by the war. Of course other industries have felt the effect, because the farmers could not produce from the soil the amount of wealth they had been producing, and could not give the factories of this country the orders they needed so much.
We have embarked upon an immigration policy with the idea of building up Canada and of filling up its vast spaces. With that policy I agree. But when we get immigrants it is necessary to supply them with work. It is not' coal miners for Nova Scotia or the western provinces that we need, or artisans. We require the class of immigrants that will go on the land and produce. There is plenty of land available in western Canada and plenty of work for immigrants of the right class, and there are still many farms in eastern Canada that should attract agriculturists from other lands. So there ought to be no difficulty in these newcomers making good homes for themselves, or in making a success of agriculture provided this basic industry is placed on a fifty-fifty basis with other industries in Canada. After we have secured these immigrants, and they have started to work,
then we must secure markets for their products. The securing of markets is important, probably more important than securing the immigrants, because if there are not markets for the products of these people they will not stay long with us. What is more, we need profitable markets. I will leave this part of my subject for the moment, and return to the question of markets a little later on.
The industrial depression in Canada, of which we have heard so much during the present session, has been due greatly, I think, to the depreciation in the value of the agriculturist's dollar. We worked hard to produce wealth, and at the end of the year when we balanced our accounts we found we were no better off. We kept at it for a number of years, and then began to inquire what was the matter. We commenced to look around. We found that the bed on which we slept enjoyed a protective duty of thirty per cent. All our clothing and all our furniture were protected to the extent of thirty-five per cent. Our agricultural machinery has a protection of from seven and a half per cent to seventeen and a half per cent according to the character of the implement. Our harness, in fact everything that we use on the farm, is protected. We apply our brains and our brawn to the cultivation of the soil and we produce beef, pork, grain, and other commodities which we have to sell on the world's markets. With the duties as they are we realize that we are greatly handicapped, and if the Progressive party stands for anything it stands for a gradual lowering of the protection of which I have spoken, so that those engaged in the great basic industry of agriculture can compete successfully in the markets of the world. If we were placed in a position to do this, such a flood of orders would pour from the farming sections of Canada into the manufacturing centres as would cause the manufacturers to forget all about a protective tariff; they would not need it then. But we are starting at the wrong end. We are building up the structure before we have constructed the foundations.
There is another thing that has entered very materially into the cost of production in Canada. I am not offering this as any argument for my remarks to-night, but I make reference to it because I think something could be done in this direction. I refer to the costs of distribution in Canada. I have before me a little memorandum containing the price of a few articles sold in the west as compared with the manufacturer's price for the same articles in eastern Canada. For one of these articles the price charged in western Canada is from
The Budget-Mr. Fansher

$2.75 to $2.85, whereas the manufacturer's price is $1.38, a difference of $1.47. In the case of a second article, which is used in all Canadian homes, the cost to the manufacturer is a little less than $55, whereas the retail price to us is over $110. I make these references because I think they will have some effect on my argument as to what we are doing to help ourselves in western Canada. We studied the tariff, we studied the cost of distributing goods from the manufacturing centres of Canada, and also what it cost to distribute farm products, and it led us up to the point where we formed an organization that is known probably all over Canada and in a good many parts of the world-I refer to the wheat pool. We found from our study of the situation as it existed in the marketing of wheat and other grains that there was a great discrepancy between the price which we received and the price which the consumer paid. So we thought out the plan of forming this wheat pool and getting our products on the world's markets at the lowest possible cost. As a result of this I can say that outside of the physical handling charges it has cost us less than a cent a bushel, we market our wheat at a saving, in some instances on the lower grades of wheat all the way from a few cents to a sum as high as thirty-one cents a bushel and possibly higher. I wish to point out that we are doing all we can by this means to increase the value of our dollar, so to speak. We are enhancing the net return to ourselves in the manner indicated. The two articles to which I refer are produced in eastern Canada-

speechtext: Name them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not wish to name
them. I can give the names of the articles and the prices privately to any hon. member who wishes that information, but I do not desire to make a public statement because that would not be fair to the parties concerned. I would point out that we farmers of western Canada have gone a long way to make the purchasing power of our dollar one hundred per cent, and I will throw out the challenge to the industrial magnates, as I may call them of the manufacturing centres of Canada, that they do something from their end of the business and give us the products of their factories at the least possible cost of distribution. Perhaps it is not a fair thing to put up to them, because they manufacture so many different things, of such different natures, that they would not be able to do as we have done with wheat. If that is the case, if it is not possible for them to do so-as some of them have suggested to me-then it is

up to us to go further and organize our purchasing power.
I stated a few moments ago that when we got immigrants of the class who could go on the farm and they began to produce, we would need markets for the products of their labour, and I want to quote a few figures showing that outside of the United States Great Britain is our best market for our products. There is a great difference between the amount of goods we import from and the amount we export to Great Britain. The figures will be shown by the following table: .
Year	Imports	Exports1923	
$141,330,143	$379,067,4451924	
153,586,690	360,057,7821925	
151,083,946	395,483,433
I quote these figures to show that we are importing from Great Britain less than half the amount we export to that market, and I want to draw some conclusions from this fact. I wish to give two illustrations which occurred in very recent history, well within the memory of any young man who is within my hearing. Hon. members will remember some few years ago that Great Britain was short of rubber. The United States had a corner on rubber, and as a result _of that condition British rubber manufacturers were somewhat handicapped. It was not, however, as large an industry then as it is now. They proceeded, therefore, to evolve a plan whereby they could supply themselves with rubber. I do not need to relate all that took place in this connection, because the facts are well known. But I want to make a reference to one other article, to show the efficiency of British capital in dealing with a situation of this kind and to indicate the manner in which an application of the same principle may be made to our wheat market.
For a time this rubber question caused the British industry some concern. But hon. members know what has happened in this connection in recent years. British financiers proceeded to plant rubber in every section of the empire in which it could be grown, and the result is that to-day seventy per cent of the entire rubber production of the world is controlled by British finance. In fact they so efficiently control it that prominent citizens of the United States have stated that England is paying off her war debt to that country out of the bounties on rubber. So much for the efficiency of the British financiers in regard to the rubber question. The same thing happened in respect to cotton. The United States at one time produced the greater portion of the world's supply of cotton, and the consequence was that Great Britain found herself short of a sufficient

The Budget-Mr. Fansher
supply to keep her mills running. In order to take care of this condition the British government proceeded to build great dams across the river Nile for the purpose of providing irrigation for the waste deserts of Egypt, which, it was proved, could produce the best cotton in the world, so that in a few years they will be able to supply themselves with their own raw material.
Hon. members may ask, what has this to do with the question before the House at the moment? Well, this is what it has to do with it. When Ramsay MacDonald was in power in Great Britain he sent a commission over to Russia to investigate trade conditions there, and investigations and negotiations have been going on to some extent ever since. To-day the Prime Minister of Great Britain has two delegates in Russia inquiring into conditions with a view to the supplying of British goods to the Russian peasant in exchange for the wheat which he produces. The expert economic adviser of the Prime Minister of Great Britain is now at the head of the commission consolidating the co-operatives there, so that they will be able to carry out this proposition. I may be asked, what has that to do with Canada? Well it has this to do with Canada; if Russia supplies Great Britain with wheat and Great Britain supplies Russia with manufactured goods, what are we going to do with our wheat? Great Britain has been taking and will continue to take our wheat until such time as Russia can produce enough to supply the British market. Britain has been taking enormous quantities of wheat and flour from Canada-not all directly from Canada, because a considerable quantity of Canadian wheat is ground in the United States and shipped from there to the British market; yet it is the Canadian product, produced on Canadian farms.
The figures which I have quoted as to the exports and imports between Great Britain and Canada show that our imports from Great Britain are so small compared with our exports to them that British financiers are getting tired of the position in which we stand, taking from them, as we do, less than half the value of our exports to them. They will probably do just as they did in the rubber and cotton industries; they will turn their attention to Russia, and they will secure from that country the wheat which they so much need for their home consumption. What is the use of bringing immigrants to this country and putting them on the land to produce, if we do not look well to the holding of that market for our products in the
future? I think we should make every effort possible to take more goods from Great Britain so that she will be in a better position to take the products of our farms.
Some hon. members have argued in this House that we do not need to take imports for exports. But let me point out that if I produce wheat or other agricultural products, they are the product of my labour. Some hon. members say that when that product goes over to Great Britain it can be paid for in gold. That is all very well, but that wheat or other agricultural product is of no value until it is consumed, and who consume it? Industrial workers consume it. And how do they pay for it? They pay for it with the product of the labour of their hands, the same as I pay with the product of the labour of my hands for the things I buy. They have to produce goods to pay for what I produce and export to them, and if I cease to take their goods they will cease to take mine.
I think I have shown in a few brief remarks that we must do something pretty soon in regard to our British market or we may lose a large portion of it to the Russian people. The trade commissioner from Russia to the United States was at St. Paul when that general conference of representatives of different countries in regard to marketing the products of the farm, or what we might call the great pool conference was held there. He made the statement that they would have 200,000,000 bushels of wheat for export next year and that before 1930 they would have reached their pre-war standard of 500,000,000 bushels of wheat. This is something that we should not treat lightly; we should do all in our power to retain the British market so that we may have at least a reasonable chance of exporting our surplus farm products. True it is that we are developing markets in other parts of the world. Some of our wheat is going to Japan and China, some to South America, and possibly in the not distant future the United States will be compelled to come to Canada for some of the wheat she needs for her great nation.
In connection with the tariff on automobiles, I wish to deal with the question of trucks. I think it was in 1917, When the greater production campaign was on, that farm tractors under $1,400 in value were admitted into Canada free. I think trucks of a large tonnage should be admitted into Canada free. In Canada we have no manufacturers of this style of truck and I will explain why I think these trucks should be admitted into Canada free. We have in western Canada a vast railway system, in fact two systems, but they

The Budget-Mr. Fansher
do not cover the entire country. There are on each side of our railway lines tremendous stretches of land that are non-productive because it is almost impossible to farm in that land and draw the product to market at a greater distance than fifteen miles from a railway. Some are drawing their grain twenty miles and some further, but that is not profitable. My contention is that trucks of a five-ton capacity could bring in the products of farms thirty miles away to those lines of railway as profitably as a farmer can now draw his grain with horses fifteen miles. This would widen the territory of production on those branch lines; it would practically double the quantity of traffic those roads would have to haul. That, I think, would be a very simple solution of part of our railway problem. This idea has not been advanced in the House before to my knowledge, but it is one that came to my mind several months ago.
The United States has often been referred to as being a very rich country and its high tariff has been advanced as the reason for that. That is a matter of opinion. The United States comprises the largest population and the greatest area of free trade country in the world, and that fact has contributed very largely to its success. In other words, it has become very rich and well established as a nation probably above all others because of its unique position in having such a large stretch of country within which free trade exists.
But another thing that has not been mentioned before that has been one of the greatest factors in the advancement of the United States in the last few years is their improved banking system. I have no quarrel with the Canadian banks as they now exist. They manufacture money, I was going to say, and turn it out to us for use, but I believe it is principally for the good of the banks. In comparing the two systems I would say that the banking system of the United States excels that of Canada in that it is useful to the common people; it has given them a chance to buy, to sell, to produce, and the United States have prospered more from that cause in the last eight or nine years than owing to their protective tariff or their unique position in being practically a self-contained country having a tropical climate in the south and also the northern climate of the great wheat belt.
I want to make one more comparison before I take my seat. I have often thought of Canada as a young giant. We know that the young men and young women of these days have rather insatiable appetites and they often
[Mr Fansher.]
slake those appetites to their own detriment. A young person to be strong and vigorous must adhere to certain rules governing the appetite, the digestive organs and so on. This young giant of Canada has had its tastes pampered to a very large extent. It has stuffed its stomach, as it were, the central provinces, and it has caused gout in its feet down by the Atlantic and an anaemic condition in the great arms of production in western Canada. The diet on which this young giant has been fed during the past number of years has contributed very largely to that situation and that is the diet of the old National Policy. I would suggest a change in the diet of this young giant so that the lifeblood may pulsate from one coast to the other. I would suggest that the rations of the old National Policy be decreased gradually and that there be substituted for that the new national policy as propounded by the Progressive party. In that way, we would have a strong, vigorous country, well able to take care of itself in the competition that is now becoming so keen with other countries of the world.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not
intend to take much of the time of this h>on. House, however, I deem it my duty to express the great satisfaction felt by the electors of the beautiful and large county of L'Assomption and Montcalm in regard to the budget speech lately delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). Moreover from one end of the country to the other, since the budget has been brought down, numerous and very clear signs of approbation have come as an endorsation of the stand which the government has taken. The budget speech characterizes well the Liberal policy which lends itself to the needs of the people and knows how to put forth, notwithstanding the protests of interested financial and manufacturing groups, a wise legislation, far-seeing and devised toward protecting the interests of the great majority of the people of the country.
The most striking points in the budget speech are the following:	A surplus of
$55,000,000; a reduction of $22,353,000 in the public debt; revenues estimated at $376,800,000 for the fiscal year 1925-26; a decrease of taxes estimated at about $25,000,000; a substantial reduction in the income tax affecting particularly the small wage earners and the head of families; the disappearance of the stamp duty on receipts; a cutting down and further exemption in connection with the sales tax; a reduction of

The Budget

Mr. Segvin
the duty on automobiles; conditional drawbacks allowed on material entering into the manufacture of automobiles; penny postage on letters; balance of trade in our favour amounting to more than $402,695,000, the largest since the war is over; British preferential tariff applied to goods transported directly into the country without being reshipped.
This is, I think, one of the most democratic budgets that we have had for a number of years, if indeed such an instance can be found in the fiscal history of our country since Confederation.
The present government through the mouthpiece of their Minister of Finance, have clearly and precisely defined the policy which they intend to follow, in order to lighten as much as possible the people's burden while providing sufficient revenues to balance the budget and meet the national indebtedness. The present government is proceeding strictly on the lines of the Liberal policy which were laid down, by the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Always anxious to give full and entire justice to all the provinces and to grant the utmost privileges, in keeping with the exceptional conditions prevailing in our country, the government has striven to give to all groups and to all parties in the country, as well as to all classes, the greatest possible measure of favours.
The government's ultimate aim, so far as the situation created by war allows, has been to unceasingly endeavour to bring down the cost of living by lowering the customs duties wherever it was possible, without endangering the life of the industries which are essential to the economic structure of the country.	It has also directed its efforts
towards reducing the cost of production in the basic industries, by allowing a freer entry into the country of the raw material essential to these industries. The government has endeavoured to contribute as much as possible to the lowering of the cost of living; and that is why the tariff has been reduced to such an extent on a great number of articles which are not produced in our country, as well as on certain tropical fruit, also on ginger, spices, cane sugar and sponges; this will enable the Canadian people to effect a saving of many thousands of dollars yearly in the home.
Mr. Speaker, the marked reduction in the tariff on automobiles valued at $1,200 or less is a further proof that the government is endeavouring to unburden the people. The automobile industry, in Canada, if we are to believe the statistics which have been 14011-191
published of late by most of the financial newspapers, has realized substantial profits. It was but right, therefore, to reduce the tariff on automobiles so as to bring down the price for the Canadian consumer. To-day, the automobile has become an entirely indispensable accessory in the commercial and social life of the people, and the farming class itself is, perhaps, the one which will benefit the most from the reduction in the tariff.
The lowering of .the tariff on tin which is not produced in our country will allow the manufacture of tin cans at a lower cost and be a factor in reducing the cost of living. This is a further proof of the Liberal government's earnest desire for the welfare of the people and its endeavour to lift the burdens which the war has accumulated upon their shoulders.
The doing away with the receipt tax, the reduction in the income tax, and the sales tax in certain cases, are so many measures which the public highly welcome. An effort was made in certain quarters to rouse the workmen of automobile factories. The untimely announcement of the closing of the works of the General Motors, at Oshawa, did certainly create a sensation; however, the reconsidering of this decision taken with the sole aim of embarrassing the government has produced the opposite effect and has shown up the bad faith of the protectionists. We must not forget that the automobile industry in our country is made up, in general, only of American branch establishments which control the market without any other competition than that which may exist between them. We must neither forget that most of these branches were established in this country in order to take advantage of the British preferential tariff and allow them to reap greater profits on their exports.
One will recall that last year, when the reduction in duties on farming implements took place, the same protests were registered, the same warnings of disaster were given by these Tory prophets. Yet the manufacturers of farming implements continued to prosper and some of them even increased their profits notwithstanding this reduction in the tariff.
Last year, like to-day, Sir, we were given to understand that the industries so affected would close their doors, that a large number of workmen would be thrown on the street, that the trekking of our people across the borders would increase in a more alarming proportion. What was the outcome of these warnings of disaster?

The Budget-Mr. Seguin

The manufacturers of automobiles have realized millions in profits, thanks to the high protective and preferential tariffs. Is it fair that these manufacturers, for the most part Americans should continue to amass wealth in such a scandalous way at the expense of the Canadian people? Is it fair that the difference between the sales price in the United States and in Canada exists simply because of the high tariff which has, up to now, allowed Canadian manufacturers to demand exorbitant prices for their cars? The difference in these prices does not only apply to touring cars, but also and especially to tractors and motor trucks. Owing to this high protective tariff, the Canadian farmer found himself at a disadvantage in relation to the American farmer. The same could be said for the manufacturer, the contractor and the trades people who made use of motor trucks in their business.
The reduction, Sir, in the income tax and the changes brought on in its administration also receive the public's sanction. Hence, the government gives further proof of its desire to lighten the people's burden. It is but fair that the business man who draws dividends from his investments, should not be placed on the same footing as the wage earner, who gets a living by the sweat of his brow. In most cases the people with independent means live on their income without being of any benefit to the community, while the wage earner is an asset owing to his work. Was it not but fair to establish a difference between the two in regard to the inoome tax?
What do yiou think now of the return to the penny postage? Is it not true to state that this measure is purely a Liberal conception, and that there does not exist one person in the whole Dominion who will not feel its good effects? Might I suggest to the hon. Minister of Finance, in order to commemorate with still more joy Dominion Day, that in making the first issue of these postage stamps they be made bilingual, thus doing justice to the two official languages recognized by the constitution of the country.
Are not all the changes, Sir, announced in' the budget speech of a nature to spread joy among all classes of society, as well as being a final answer to the whisper of death? It is, therefore, with confidence that the Canadian people can look forward to the future, now that the Liberal party, with the help of Providence no doubt, has succeeded in bringing prosperity to our country which the evil Borden-Meighen governments seemed to have banished forever. As a whole, the budget seems to meet the public's approval, if we make an exception for those who are

directly affected or are blinded by their political passions. Judging from the measures brought down, the Liberal party once more has emphasized the policy it intends to follow, which has been that of its leaders for the last thirty years past. It is the golden mean between high protection and free trade. It is the wisest policy for a country like ours, it is the only policy which acknowledges the rights of the people in every part of our vast country. It is this constructive policy that the people endorsed at the last general elections, it is that policy that the province of Quebec approved by its vote. And it is for toe pursuance of this beneficial policy that I shall register my vote in favour of the budget resolutions, as submitted by the hon. Minister of Finance.
I think, Sir, that it will be to the satisfaction of everybody if, at this late hour, I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
